fr.elements: Main Building; Front Driveway; Access Road; Open Green Space; Landscaped Area; Dense Vegetation; Street Frontage; Perimeter Fencing; Open Terrain; Detached Structure
fr.considerations: Single Access Point; Long Driveway; Dense Vegetation; Limited Rear Access; Open Terrain
fr.recommendations: Providing a clearly marked address visible from the street and at the driveway entrance could significantly improve response times given the single access point and extended driveway length. Ensuring the driveway remains wide enough to accommodate emergency vehicles and allows for turnaround or staging near the main building would support effective operations, particularly where rear access is limited. Keeping the driveway and any pathways between the main building and detached structure clear of encroaching vegetation could improve both navigation and aerial visibility for responding personnel. A secondary egress path, where feasible within the property, may further enhance responder and occupant movement options during an emergency.

wildfire.conditions: Structure Surrounded by Vegetation; Scattered Shrubs; Scattered Trees; Tree Cluster; Dense Shrub Cover; Brush Adjacent to Structure; Fuel Continuity; Brushland Interface; Mixed Vegetation Cover; Open Terrain; Single Access Route; Wildland Interface
wildfire.recommendations: Reducing brush directly adjacent to the structure and creating greater separation between shrubs, tree clusters, and the building perimeter could meaningfully improve defensible space and reduce fuel continuity around the improvements. Where dense shrub cover and mixed vegetation connect from the surrounding brushland toward the structure, thinning and separating those fuels may reduce the opportunity for fire to carry close to the building. Maintaining spacing between individual shrubs and between shrubs and any overhanging tree canopy would further support fuel continuity reduction across the property. Given the single access route serving the property, keeping that corridor clear of encroaching vegetation on both sides would support firefighter access and improve conditions for suppression operations. Preserving and expanding any open terrain near the structure as a buffer zone, and continuing to manage vegetation concentrations within the immediate structure perimeter, would support long-term wildfire resilience and improve overall property preparedness at this wildland interface location.
